name: Gum recession treatment

image.caption: Receding Gums or Gingival Recession, Causes, and Treatment

lead: Gum recession treatment covers procedures that cover exposed roots and rebuild the gumline, mainly gum grafts from the palate or a donor matrix, plus flap techniques and growth-factor products. The payoff is shorter-looking teeth, an even gumline and a more natural smile.

Tissue is moved, grafted or regenerated over the exposed root and secured while it heals over about two to four weeks. Recession is very common: one meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources estimates about 85 percent of people worldwide have it on at least one tooth. Many registered trials compare grafts with collagen membranes, platelet-rich fibrin, placental membrane and other techniques.

paras: A periodontist chooses a technique based on how much recession there is and the bone and gum support. Treating the cause, such as gum disease, tooth position or brushing habits, is done alongside covering the root. Healing takes about two to four weeks.

Expect soreness, sensitivity and swelling while it heals, plus donor-site discomfort when palate tissue is used. Outcomes vary by technique and bone support, and if the cause of recession is not treated it can return.

angle.text: People treat gum recession, mostly with grafts, to cover exposed roots and restore an even gumline so teeth look natural in length. The visible coverage is the result of the procedure, and techniques are widely studied with results that vary.

lead: Gum recession treatment refers to the procedures used to restore or cover gum that has pulled back from the teeth and exposed the roots. Recession is common: one meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources estimates that about 85 percent of people worldwide have it on at least one tooth, and a 2026 study puts the figure at roughly 81 percent.[1][2] Periodontal disease is its most common cause.[1]

Options include pedicle grafts, free gingival and connective tissue grafts, acellular dermal matrix, and growth-factor techniques; healing takes about two to four weeks.[1] Studies and registered trials compare grafts with collagen membranes, platelet-rich fibrin, placental membrane and other techniques.[3][4][5][6]
infobox: Pedicle graft, free gingival graft, connective tissue graft, dermal matrix

paras: Periodontal disease is the most common cause. Other reported causes include aggressive brushing, thin gum tissue, tobacco, trauma, crowded teeth and piercings; evidence linking brushing to recession is described as inconclusive.[1]

A periodontist can regenerate gum tissue using nearby tissue, palatal grafts or a donor dermal matrix, usually under local anaesthesia. Growth-factor-infused bone graft material is another option described.[1] Complete or near-complete coverage is described as possible when there is no periodontal bone loss, though that statement is marked as needing citation.[1] A trial of Russian origin examined autogenous oral mucosa fibroblast injections, reporting increased gum thickness and reduced recession for at least nine months.[7]

Registered trials compare a xenogenic collagen membrane with connective tissue graft,[3] platelet-rich fibrin with connective tissue graft and coronally advanced flap alone,[6] coronally advanced flap with or without PRF,[4] placental membrane for root coverage,[5] de-epithelialised free gingival graft[8] and cyanoacrylate adhesive versus suture.[9] Results are not summarised here.
A 2026 cross-sectional analysis evaluated the reliability and educational value of YouTube videos on gingival recession and its management.[2]
